l4hu-bn-opening: Opening Nearly 100%: The Button Attack in Heads-Up

In heads-up the button (SB) opens preflop and only acts last once the flop arrives. Against a single opponent the opening frequency can approach 100% — only a handful of total junk hands (72o, 83o) are folded. The reason: the SB only completes 0.5 to see a 1.5BB pot (25% equity needed), so almost every hand is at or above that line against a wide defense range; and (acting last postflop with position) the initiative extends through the last two streets. Opening wide is not "playing loose", it is "squeezing every marginal EV with frequency".

The core of button opening is "sizing serves postflop", not "sizing serves stealing". Heads-up you mostly use min-raise (2BB): the steal threshold is low (50% fold rate needed), the small size keeps the pot controllable postflop, and a wide enough range covers every board.
The Math of Opening Sizes: Why min-raise Is the Main Weapon

Math of a SB min-raise to 2BB (SB has 0.5 in, adds 1.5BB; BB has 1 in, may fold or add 1):

Pure-steal model (BB folding as the baseline, the 0.5 dead money is sunk):
BB folds -> SB collects the current 1.5BB pot; BB calls -> SB loses the extra 1.5BB
EV(raise) = f x 1.5 - (1 - f) x 1.5 (f = BB fold rate)
Break-even: f = 1.5/(1.5+1.5) = 50%

So once the BB folds more than 50%, the SB profits automatically with any two cards on a min-raise.
Size comparison: min-raise 2BB -> 50%; 2.5BB (adds 2) -> 2/3.5 = about 57.1%; 3BB (adds 2.5) -> 2.5/4 = 62.5%.

Plugging fold rates in: f = 0.35 (BB defends 65%) -> 0.35 x 1.5 - 0.65 x 1.5 = -0.45BB;
f = 0.55 -> 0.55 x 1.5 - 0.45 x 1.5 = +0.15BB.

Conclusion: the bigger the size, the higher the auto-profit threshold. Heads-up the opening value sits postflop, so the smaller size keeps the pot controllable.

Why not copy the full-ring idea that "stealing needs a bigger size"? Three reasons: (1) the BB only folds about 30%-40% against a min-raise heads-up, so a pure steal barely breaks even and the value is postflop; (2) a big size is self-punishment heads-up — the BB calling range narrows with the size, so 3BB buys you only a stronger calling range; (3) frequency and balance — min-raise lets you open roughly 80% of hands, and only a wide range covers every postflop board.

Example: heads-up 100BB deep, you (SB) hold QdJd. This is a marginal hand from an early full-ring seat, but heads-up the equity is about 52% against a wide defending range, so a 2BB min-raise is a standard open. Postflop you also act last, and QJs is a clear open here.

Example 2 (fold rate decides whether to size up): you observe the BB folding 55% against a min-raise. The pure-steal EV is 0.55 x 1.5 - 0.45 x 1.5 = +0.15BB, just past the 50% break-even line. That is still no reason to size up: the same fold rate against a 2.5BB open needs 2/3.5 = about 57.1% to break even, so 55% is not enough and the steal turns negative. Sizing is decided by postflop pot control, not by the fold rate.

Counterintuitive point: "opening nearly 100%" on the heads-up button is not greed, it is math. But notice — a wide open does not mean putting money in on every street, nor does it mean opening 100% against every opponent. Once the 3-bet frequency rises, the marginal hands pushed out of your opening range multiply quickly and the frequency must come back down.

Theory support: why the heads-up opening range can be as wide as 80%-100% is covered in Theory Academy T4 "Range Width" — that chapter turns "only one opponent" and "position reversal" into a computable equity account, and this lesson's opening frequency is a corollary.

Theory support: how much frequency min-raise, 3-bet and 4-bet each need in order to be indifferent is covered in Theory Academy T5 "Heads-Up Preflop Equilibrium" — that chapter derives participation and defense rates from price lines with the indifference principle, and this lesson's 50% break-even fold rate is one of those lines.

Button open cheat sheet: default min-raise 2BB over roughly 80%-100% of hands; mix the top 15% strong hands, the middle suited connectors and Ax, and the bottom junk. Every 50 hands, check: is the 3-bet from the opponent pushing you out of your opening range? Does the fold rate still support opening 100%?

Button opening in three lines:
The break-even fold rate for a 2BB min-raise is 50% (1.5 / 3); sizing up to 2.5BB needs 57.1% and 3BB needs 62.5%
The BB really folds about 30%-40%, so a pure steal is often negative (f = 0.35 gives -0.45BB); the profit comes from postflop position and range width
Raise the opening frequency as the fold rate rises, lower it as the 3-bet frequency rises, and always size for postflop pot control
l4hu-ev-adjustments: Heads-Up Pots: Simpler EV, Amplified Numbers

Heads-up only ever has two-way pots, so the EV math is simpler than full-ring, but the numbers mean more. Simpler: no multiway dilution and no "this out gives another opponent a flush", so your win rate is closer to "equity against one range". Amplified: the dead-money share is high (SB 0.5) and the opponent range is wide, so the same EV edge repeats at a high frequency and compounds into a larger long-run gain. Understanding these two shifts is the core of EV adjustment heads-up.

The core EV formula is unchanged, but the inputs are clearer: EV(call) = E x (P+B) - (1-E) x B. What differs is "wider opponent range, higher dead-money share", which turns many marginal calls into +EV.
Preflop Steal EV and Postflop Positional EV

Preflop steal EV (SB min-raises to 2BB, BB fold rate f, folding as the baseline):
EV(steal) = f x 1.5 - (1-f) x 1.5 (break-even f = 50%)

Postflop positional EV anchor:
heads-up position is worth about 0.5-1BB per hand (SB acts last postflop)

Worked example: the BB faces a SB min-raise (SB has 2BB in total, the BB already has 1BB in):
General form: required equity = call / (current pot + opponent bet + call)
Plug in: 1 / (1.5 + 1.5 + 1) = 1 / 4 = 25%
(current pot 1.5 = SB 0.5 + the 1 the BB itself put in; that 1BB is dead money but still belongs in the denominator — never drop it. Opponent bet 1.5 = what the SB adds to reach 2BB; call 1 = what the BB must add. Equivalently the pot after the call is 4BB and 1/4 = 25%.)
Against a SB opening range of about 80%, marginal hands often have more than 40% equity -> calling is +EV

Same formula postflop (pot before the bet P, opponent bet b):
half pot (P=4, b=2): 2 / (4 + 2 + 2) = 25%
1/3 pot (P=6, b=2): 2 / (6 + 2 + 2) = 20%
pot-sized (P=4, b=4): 4 / (4 + 4 + 4) = 33.3%

EV(call) cross-check: E x (P+B) - (1-E) x B
E=30%, P=4, B=2 -> 0.30 x 6 - 0.70 x 2 = 1.8 - 1.4 = +0.4BB

What this means in practice: against the wide SB range the BB calling threshold drops sharply. A 40% calling line against a 15% UTG range in full-ring becomes 25% heads-up against an 80% SB range (1BB more into a 4BB pot after the call), and against a range that wide the marginal hands themselves have more real equity. That is why the BB can defend 60%+ heads-up — not "loose", but "the result of the EV math".

Example: 0.5/1 blinds, the SB min-raises to 2BB and you (BB) hold Ks7s. Calling costs 1BB and the pot after the call is SB 2 + BB 1 already in + your 1 = 4BB, so required equity = 1 / 4 = 25%. K7s has about 48% against a SB range of roughly 80%, a surplus of about 23 points. Postflop you check first and mostly check-call: a K gives thin value, flushes and straights come cheap, and total misses can be abandoned. The call is +EV — K7s folds against UTG in full-ring, but heads-up against a wide SB range it is a +EV call.

Example 2 (postflop EV): on a 4BB flop pot the BB checks and the SB bets 2BB (half pot). Required equity = 2 / (4 + 2 + 2) = 25%. Your 76 on 9s8d3c has a double gutshot plus a backdoor flush draw, about 8 outs and 17% for one street — short of 25% on its own, but with implied odds (another 2.5BB when the straight arrives) the call turns +EV. Heads-up draws lean on implied odds more often because the opponent range is wide and willing to pay.

Counterintuitive point: small hands are not junk heads-up. Nine-high can still win a postflop pot — the calling range is so wide that nine-high showdown value far exceeds full-ring. At the same 25% pot odds, nine-high may be ahead 40%+ of the time heads-up versus 15%-20% in full-ring.

Theory support: comparing the fold / call / raise branches and quantifying positional value is covered in Theory Academy T2 "Expected Value Optimization" — this lesson moves that framework into two-way pots and recalibrates the inputs with dead-money share and opponent range width.

Theory support: pricing risk for the postflop out-of-position side and how implied odds shift is covered in Theory Academy T2 "Risk Assessment" — heads-up draws lean on implied odds precisely because a wide range crushes single-street equity.

Heads-up EV quick anchors: half-pot bets need 25% equity, 1/3 pot 20%, pot-sized 33.3%; limping to see a flop 25%, calling a 3BB open 33.3%. Memorise these and the table math gets faster than counting.

Heads-up EV in three lines:
Calling line = call / pot after the call, and the denominator must include your own dead money (min-raise: 1 / 4 = 25%)
Size sets the threshold: half pot 25%, 1/3 pot 20%, pot-sized 33.3% — memorise the three tiers
A positional value of 0.5-1BB per hand is a long-run expectation that belongs to the side holding position, not a per-hand guarantee
l4hu-gto-basics: Heads-Up: The Purest Setting for Equilibrium Play

Heads-up poker (ignoring rake) is a pure two-player zero-sum game, so the Nash equilibrium guarantee of being unexploitable holds exactly. That means a GTO strategy exists: however the opponent plays, your long-run expectation does not drop below the game value. Compared with full-ring, heads-up GTO ranges are extremely wide (SB opens about 80%, BB defends 60%+), and equilibrium implies very high betting frequency and bluff density — GTO is not "playing tight", it is "keeping everything at a ratio the opponent cannot counter".

GTO is a bulletproof vest, not a weapon: it guarantees you are not exploited, but it does not promise maximum profit. Against leaky opponents, targeted exploitation earns more — at the cost of opening your own leaks. Strong heads-up players switch between wearing the vest and drawing the knife.
Frequency Benchmarks: Value-to-Bluff Ratio and MDF

Equilibrium value-to-bluff ratio for a pot-sized river bet (pot P, bet P):
bluff share f = b/(1+2b) = 1/(1+2) = 1/3
so value:bluff = 2:1.

Half pot (b=0.5): f = 0.5/2 = 25%, value:bluff = 3:1.
Two times pot (b=2): f = 2/(1+4) = 40%, value:bluff = 3:2.

MDF (minimum defence frequency) = 1/(1+b):
1/3 pot -> 75%; half pot -> 67%; pot-sized -> 50%; two times pot -> 33%.

Heads-up the BB defends 60%+, far above the MDF floor (about 33%-38%), because acting last preflop and the dead money already in make calling +EV on its own.

How heads-up GTO differs from full-ring frequencies: in full-ring most seats can only play tight and equilibrium betting frequency is low; heads-up the ranges are wide, betting frequency is high and bluff density is large. Solvers output plenty of aggressive betting and polarized ranges heads-up. Understanding these benchmarks is the precondition for spotting when the opponent leaves equilibrium.

Example: heads-up SB against BB, the solver tells you the SB opens about 80% of hands and the BB defends about 60%+, with the out-of-position BB checking at a high frequency and the in-position SB betting at a high frequency postflop. These frequencies look loose but are all part of equilibrium — if either side deviates (say the SB only opens 50%), the other can exploit it by widening its defence or raising its steal frequency.

Example 2 (positional symmetry): every heads-up hand swaps SB and BB, so position is not fixed — the SB opens preflop and only acts last once the flop arrives, while the BB is the mirror image. A GTO equilibrium contains strategies for both positional directions, so positional symmetry means you must be able to play both seats and cannot carry over the full-ring idea of a fixed seat.

Counterintuitive point: "GTO means playing tight" is the biggest misreading. Heads-up GTO is full of high-frequency betting, overbet shoves and thin value — it only keeps them at ratios the opponent cannot counter. When studying solvers, do not memorise frequencies; ask three whys: why this size on this board? why does this hand enter the betting range? why did the frequency change on the turn?

Theory support: unexploitability, game value and the idea that "GTO is not the most profitable" are covered in Theory Academy T5 "Core Ideas of GTO" — this lesson's frequency benchmarks are the practical version of that chapter's "equilibrium only guarantees the floor".

Theory support: mixed strategies, the indifference principle and the critical-frequency maths behind MDF and Alpha are covered in Theory Academy T5 "Frequency Balance" — value:bluff 2:1 and MDF 50% are two faces of the same equation.

Heads-up GTO study path: first use a solver to understand the shape of equilibrium (why it plays this way), then use node locking to study how to harvest the opponent's common leaks, and finally verify in play. The baseline keeps you un-exploitable; deviations supply the profit margin.

Heads-up GTO in three lines:
Equilibrium guarantees the floor of not being exploited, not the ceiling of maximum profit
Benchmarks are recomputable: value:bluff 2:1 pot-sized, 3:1 half pot, 3:2 two times pot; MDF = 1/(1+b) (1/3 pot 75%, half pot 67%, pot-sized 50%, two times pot 33%)
The BB closes the preflop action and its dead money makes calling cheap, which is why it can defend above the MDF floor
l4hu-counter-strategies: Spotting Deviations: The Prerequisite for Counter-Strategy

Counter-strategy heads-up means: first identify the tendency by which the opponent leaves equilibrium, then use the GTO baseline to calibrate the best response to that leak. Four deviations are common heads-up: folding too much (an extremely high fold rate against continuation bets), calling too loose (a calling station), 3-betting too often, and continuation betting too often. Identification relies on frequency statistics over 50-100 hands, not on the impression from a single hand.

The right posture: aim at the leak (maximally exploitative) but keep the size minimal (minimally exploitative). Every deviation opens a leak of your own, so the size must stay controlled and you must return to baseline as soon as the opponent adjusts.
Targeted Responses to the Four Deviations

Raising the steal frequency against an over-folding opponent (SB min-raises to 2BB, BB fold rate f, folding as the baseline with the 1.5/1.5 convention):
EV(steal) = f x 1.5 - (1-f) x 1.5

Equilibrium fold rate about 40% (f=0.4) -> EV = 0.4 x 1.5 - 0.6 x 1.5 = -0.3BB (unprofitable, postflop must make up)
If the opponent folds 60% (f=0.6) -> EV = 0.6 x 1.5 - 0.4 x 1.5 = +0.3BB (the pure steal profits automatically)
If the opponent folds 70% (f=0.7) -> EV = 0.7 x 1.5 - 0.3 x 1.5 = +0.6BB (profit widens)
Extrapolating further: at f=0.5, EV = 0.5 x 1.5 - 0.5 x 1.5 = 0BB (break-even); at f=0.8, EV = 0.8 x 1.5 - 0.2 x 1.5 = +0.9BB

Conclusion: the higher the fold rate, the more you should raise the steal frequency, but only up to the point where "he can correct to 50% and you still do not lose".

Direction for the four deviations: (1) folds too much -> raise the open and continuation-bet frequency and use more semi-bluffs; (2) calls too loose (calling station) -> cut pure bluffs and switch to thin value, because even top pair with a weak kicker can bet for money; (3) 3-bets too often -> narrow the opening range and add value 4-bets; (4) continuation bets too often -> raise the check-raise frequency and float more. Each one runs the loop of identify, respond, re-check.

Example: you observe a heads-up opponent folding 60% against continuation bets (equilibrium is about 45%). That is a clear over-folding leak. Response: raise the flop continuation-bet frequency and bluff density overall, and start betting hands you used to check. The size is directly computable: pot 4BB, bet 1.33BB (1/3 pot), a 55% fold rate gives EV = 0.55 x 4 - 0.45 x 1.33 = 2.20 - 0.60 = about +1.60BB. Even so, the cap is "if he tightens to 50% you still do not lose". This is a directed, disciplined deviation from a GTO baseline based on an observable bias.

Example 2 (countering a calling station): the opponent almost never folds postflop (fold rate below 25%). Response: pure bluffs do not work because he does not fold, so switch to thin value betting — even top pair with a weak kicker bets for money because he calls with worse. Convert bluff hands into semi-bluffs or check them. A calling station is the easiest type to harvest heads-up, as long as you resist bluffing.

Example 3 (node locking in practice): use the solver to lock "this opponent folds 55% against a turn second barrel" at that fixed frequency and re-solve your best response — the solver immediately pushes your turn bluff frequency up. That is node locking turning counter-strategy from feeling into calculation.

Counterintuitive point: the biggest risk is not under-exploiting but over-exploiting and turning yourself into the leak. Strong heads-up players keep one hand on the GTO baseline steering wheel while harvesting the opponent's leaks — the moment the opponent adjusts, they snap back.

Theory support: locking the opponent's deviation at a fixed frequency and re-solving the best response is covered in Theory Academy T5 "Node Locking and Minimal Deviation" — that chapter also gives the criterion for when a deviation turns from positive to negative, and every response in this lesson is capped by it.

Theory support: the full framework for moving from a GTO baseline to exploitation, and the boundary at which you must return to baseline, is covered in Theory Academy T7 "Targeted Adjustments" — the four responses here are concrete instances of that framework.

Counter-strategy execution in five steps: (1) collect enough of a sample on the tracker to confirm the leak; (2) lock that node in the solver and solve the best response; (3) compare with the baseline and write down the raised frequencies and sizes; (4) execute in play; (5) re-check every 500 hands whether the sample still holds.

Heads-up counter-strategy in three lines:
Measure before countering: only fold rates and 3-bet rates over 50-100 hands count as a leak; single-hand impressions are noise
Every deviation has a direction, and the size is capped by "you still do not lose after the opponent corrects" (f=0.6 -> +0.3BB, f=0.8 -> +0.9BB)
Over-exploiting is more dangerous than under-exploiting — the moment you deviate, your own leak opens with it

l4hu-bn-opening-q1.question: The HU button (SB) opening frequency range is about:
l4hu-bn-opening-q1.explanation: The HU SB opens about 80%-100%, folding only a few completely junk hands — completing 0.5 sees a 1.5BB pot, and postflop the SB has the final word.

l4hu-bn-opening-q2.question: Why does the HU button open mainly with min-raise (2BB)?
options: The min-raise steal bar is low (50% fold rate) and postflop pot control is easier
The min-raise makes the opponent fold more easily
l4hu-bn-opening-q2.explanation: The min-raise's steal break-even is a 50% fold rate, the small size makes postflop pot control easier, and it supports a ~80% wide range. Big sizes are self-punishment in HU.

l4hu-bn-opening-q3.question: The real HU BB fold rate vs min-raise is about:
l4hu-bn-opening-q3.explanation: The HU BB's real fold rate vs min-raise is only about 30%-40% (defending 60%-70%), meaning pure stealing barely profits — the open's value is postflop.

l4hu-bn-opening-q4.question: The correct understanding of the HU button "opening about 80%" is:
options: Participate in about 80%, but many hands let go in time by postflop board fit
Only play the top 80% strong hands
l4hu-bn-opening-q4.explanation: Opening wide means "participate a lot, invest little" — letting go in time by postflop board fit is the mature play.

l4hu-bn-opening-q5.question: Facing a frequent 3-bettor (the BB), how should the button adjust its opening?
options: Narrowing the range, reducing marginal hands that only fold after a 3-bet
l4hu-bn-opening-q5.explanation: High 3-bet frequency erodes steal EV and marginal hands only fold after a 3-bet. Narrowing is correct; stopping entirely overreacts.

l4hu-bn-opening-q6.question: You (SB) size the open up from a 2BB min-raise to 2.5BB. The break-even fold rate for the pure steal becomes:
l4hu-bn-opening-q6.explanation: With the bigger size the SB adds 2BB, so break-even f = 2 / (1.5 + 2) = 2 / 3.5 = about 57.1%. 50% is the min-raise figure (1.5 / 3); 62.5% is the 3BB threshold (2.5 / 4).

l4hu-bn-opening-q7.question: The break-even fold rate for a pure steal when you open to 3BB is:
l4hu-bn-opening-q7.explanation: A 3BB open means the SB adds 2.5BB, so break-even f = 2.5 / (1.5 + 2.5) = 2.5 / 4 = 62.5%. 75% is an MDF figure (the defence line against a 1/3-pot bet) and is a different question entirely.

l4hu-bn-opening-q8.question: The BB only folds 35% against a min-raise. The EV of the pure steal is:
l4hu-bn-opening-q8.explanation: With folding as the baseline: EV = f x 1.5 - (1-f) x 1.5 = 0.35 x 1.5 - 0.65 x 1.5 = 0.525 - 0.975 = -0.45BB. +0.15BB is the result at a 55% fold rate and 0BB is the 50% break-even point.

l4hu-bn-opening-q9.question: The heads-up button still opens roughly 80%-100% of hands. The fundamental reason is:
options: only one opponent and acting last postflop amplify both the marginal-hand equity and the positional edge
the rules let the button open more often
l4hu-bn-opening-q9.explanation: Range width comes from two things: only one opponent (no multiway dilution) and acting last postflop (positional edge). Luck and rules are not reasons, and whether the opponent 3-bets only shifts the frequency, not the source of the width.

l4hu-bn-opening-q10.question: The opponent fold rate sits exactly on the break-even point. The correct reading is:
options: the pure-steal segment has zero expectation, so the whole value of opening comes postflop
you should narrow the range to 10%
you should size up to chase the opponent away
l4hu-bn-opening-q10.explanation: The break-even point means the steal segment is 0.5 x 1.5 - 0.5 x 1.5 = 0, so all the gain or loss from opening comes from postflop equity and position — which is why the range can stay wide but postflop discipline is mandatory.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q1.question: The main difference between HU and full-ring EV calculation is:
options: No multiway dilution, high dead-money share, wide opponent range — the EV numbers are amplified
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q1.explanation: The EV formula is unchanged, but HU two-player pots have no dilution, the SB's dead money share is high, and the opponent's range is wide — turning more marginal calls +EV and amplifying the meaning.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q2.question: SB min-raises to 2BB (the BB already has 1BB in); the BB still has to call 1BB. Required equity is about:
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q2.explanation: Required equity = call ÷ (current pot + opponent's bet + your call) = 1 ÷ (1.5 + 1.5 + 1) = 1 ÷ 4 = 25%. The denominator must include the BB's own 1BB already in the pot (1/(2+1) ≈ 33.3% is exactly the value you get by omitting it). HU's dead-money share is high — cheaper than the full-ring BTN call at 40%.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q3.question: The root reason the HU BB defends 60%+ is:
options: The call bar is low vs the SB's wide range, and the BB's preflop final say adds information
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q3.explanation: Vs the SB's ~80% wide range the call bar drops to 25% (1BB more into a 4BB pot after the call); the BB has the final say preflop and its dead money makes the price cheap, so it can defend wide — the result of EV calculation, not looseness. The over-100% equity-realization bonus belongs to the position-holding SB, not the BB.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q4.question: HU draw calls (like double-gutshots) rely on implied odds because:
options: The opponent's range is wide with high payment willingness — winning more when the draw hits
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q4.explanation: The HU opponent's range is wide with high payment willingness, so you win more when the draw hits (good implied odds), compensating for the single-street equity shortfall.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q5.question: HU positional value of about 0.5-1BB/hand means:
options: The BB wins 1BB more every flop
Over the long run the SB earns 0.5-1BB more expected value per hand than the BB
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q5.explanation: Positional value is a long-run expectation gap: the SB acts last postflop holding IP, averaging 0.5-1BB extra per hand — a statistical expectation, not a per-hand guarantee.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q6.question: The flop pot is 6BB and the SB bets 2BB (1/3 pot). The BB required equity to call is about:
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q6.explanation: Required equity = 2 / (6 + 2 + 2) = 2 / 10 = 20%. 25% is the half-pot figure (2 / (4+2+2)) and 33.3% is the pot-sized figure — memorising one size as a universal number is exactly the trap here.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q7.question: The pot is 4BB and the SB bets 2BB (half pot). The BB required equity to call is about:
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q7.explanation: 2 / (4 + 2 + 2) = 2 / 8 = 25%: calling 2BB buys a share of an 8BB pot, so one quarter breaks even. 40% is the full-ring rule of thumb against a tight range, which a wide heads-up range does not require.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q8.question: Facing a half-pot bet (P=4, B=2) you estimate 30% equity. Using EV(call) = E x (P+B) - (1-E) x B, the call EV is:
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q8.explanation: EV = 0.30 x (4+2) - 0.70 x 2 = 1.8 - 1.4 = +0.4BB. +1.8BB counts only the winning half and forgets the cost of calling; -1.4BB counts only the cost.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q9.question: Heads-up draws lean on implied odds more often than in full-ring. The fundamental reason is:
options: the opponent range is wide and willing to pay, so more chips come after you hit
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q9.explanation: Completion odds do not depend on the number of opponents (a flush draw is still about 35% across two streets); what differs is how many more chips you win after hitting against a wide range — implied odds fill the single-street equity gap.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q10.question: The statement "position is worth about 0.5-1BB per hand to the SB" means:
options: the SB is guaranteed 1BB more every hand
over the long run, acting last postflop lifts the SB expectation 0.5-1BB per hand above the BB
this is the preflop opening profit
the number only holds in tournaments
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q10.explanation: Positional value is a long-run expectation difference, not a per-hand guarantee: it measures the average effect of acting last postflop in turning the same cards into more chips, and it holds in both cash games and tournaments.

l4hu-gto-basics-q1.question: The applicability of the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee in HU:
options: Strictly holds (HU is a pure two-player zero-sum game)
l4hu-gto-basics-q1.explanation: HU (ignoring rake) is a pure two-player zero-sum game, where the Nash unexploitable guarantee strictly holds. Multiway pots weaken under coalition effects.

l4hu-gto-basics-q2.question: The equilibrium value:bluff ratio for a river full-pot bet is about:
l4hu-gto-basics-q2.explanation: Bluff share f = 1/(1+2) = 1/3, so 2/3 value and 1/3 bluffs, value:bluff = 2:1. Exactly equals the opponent's required call equity of 33%.

l4hu-gto-basics-q3.question: The main difference between HU GTO and full-ring GTO is:
options: HU ranges are extremely wide with high betting frequencies and bluff density
l4hu-gto-basics-q3.explanation: HU ranges are wide (SB 80%, BB 60%+), so equilibrium comes with high betting frequencies and polarized ranges — not "playing tight".

l4hu-gto-basics-q4.question: Why does the HU BB defend 60%+, far above the MDF floor (about 33%-38%)?
options: The BB has better cards every hand
The BB has the final say preflop, and its 1BB of dead money makes calling cheap
The MDF formula doesn't apply preflop
l4hu-gto-basics-q4.explanation: MDF only guarantees "stopping pure-bluff auto-profit"; the BB's positive call EV comes from having the final say preflop plus its dead-money odds, so it can defend above the floor and still profit. The over-100% equity-realization bonus belongs to the position-holding SB.

l4hu-gto-basics-q5.question: HU "positional symmetry" means:
options: Every hand the two sides swap SB/BB — you must play both the SB and the BB
l4hu-gto-basics-q5.explanation: In HU the two sides swap SB/BB every hand — the order flips (the SB opens first preflop and acts last postflop; the BB is the reverse); the GTO equilibrium includes positional strategies in both directions.

l4hu-gto-basics-q6.question: Against a half-pot bet, the opponent minimum defence frequency (MDF) is:
l4hu-gto-basics-q6.explanation: MDF = 1 / (1 + b) = 1 / 1.5 = about 66.7%. 75% is the 1/3-pot figure (1 / (1 + 1/3)) and 50% is the pot-sized figure.

l4hu-gto-basics-q7.question: The equilibrium bluff share for a half-pot bet is:
l4hu-gto-basics-q7.explanation: f = b / (1 + 2b) = 0.5 / 2 = 25%, so value:bluff = 3:1. 33.3% is the pot-sized figure (1 / 3) and 40% is the two-times-pot figure (2 / 5).

l4hu-gto-basics-q8.question: For a two-times-pot shove (b = 2), MDF and the equilibrium bluff share are:
l4hu-gto-basics-q8.explanation: MDF = 1 / (1 + 2) = 33.3%; bluff share = 2 / (1 + 4) = 40%. The two numbers are not equal: MDF says how much the opponent must defend, bluff share says how much air you carry yourself.

l4hu-gto-basics-q9.question: What positional symmetry actually demands from a learner is:
options: every hand swaps the blinds, so both positional directions must be trained to equilibrium
only drill the big blind defence
l4hu-gto-basics-q9.explanation: Every heads-up hand swaps the blinds, so position reverses and half your hands are in position while half are out of position; training one direction only leaves the other half permanently exploitable.

l4hu-gto-basics-q10.question: Calling GTO a bulletproof vest means:
options: GTO secures the floor of not being exploited; exploitation is what raises the ceiling
GTO only works in multiway pots
l4hu-gto-basics-q10.explanation: Equilibrium secures the floor of "you do not lose however the opponent plays"; the profit ceiling comes from exploiting leaks, at the cost of opening your own. The two are a division of labour, not substitutes.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q1.question: The correct basis for identifying a HU opponent's deviation is:
l4hu-counter-strategies-q1.explanation: HU countering relies on 50-100 hand frequency statistics (fold rate/3-bet rate, etc.); single-hand impressions are noise, insufficient evidence.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q2.question: Against an over-folding opponent, the correct counter is:
options: Raise open/C-Bet frequency and add semi-bluffs
l4hu-counter-strategies-q2.explanation: An over-folding opponent makes steal and C-Bet fold rates automatic profit — raise open/C-Bet frequency and semi-bluff density.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q3.question: Against a calling station who calls too loose, the correct counter is:
options: Cut bluffs and switch to value-bet thin value
l4hu-counter-strategies-q3.explanation: A station doesn't fold, so pure bluffs are useless; switch to value-bet thin value because he calls with worse hands.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q4.question: The discipline of "minimum necessary deviation" is:
options: Aiming at the opponent's leak with minimal magnitude, ready to return to baseline anytime
l4hu-counter-strategies-q4.explanation: Deviations open your own leaks, so keep the magnitude controlled; aim at the leak, keep it minimal, and return to baseline when the opponent adjusts.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q5.question: The role of node locking in countering is:
options: Locking the opponent's deviation as a fixed frequency and re-solving your optimal response
l4hu-counter-strategies-q5.explanation: Node locking feeds "how the opponent actually plays (deviation)" into the solver and outputs the optimal counter against that bias — turning countering from feel into calculation.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q6.question: When the BB fold rate against a min-raise is exactly 50%, the pure steal EV is:
l4hu-counter-strategies-q6.explanation: EV = 0.5 x 1.5 - 0.5 x 1.5 = 0BB, which is exactly the break-even point; +0.3BB corresponds to a 60% fold rate and -0.3BB to 40%.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q7.question: When the opponent fold rate rises to 80%, the pure steal EV is:

l4hu-counter-strategies-q8.question: Pot 4BB, you bet 1.33BB (1/3 pot) and the opponent folds 55%. The EV of this street is about:
l4hu-counter-strategies-q8.explanation: EV = 0.55 x 4 - 0.45 x 1.33 = 2.20 - 0.60 = about +1.60BB. +2.20BB counts only the fold profit and drops the loss when called; +1.87BB is the result at a 60% fold rate.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q9.question: Where node locking sits in the counter-strategy loop:
options: it fixes the observed deviation as a solver input and re-solves the best response to it
it locks your own action frequencies
l4hu-counter-strategies-q9.explanation: Node locking changes the opponent branch of the tree (its fold and call rates are pinned) and the solver re-solves your best action; it cannot replace a sample and it does not change the limits on your own frequencies.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q10.question: The most concrete cost of over-exploiting is:
options: you punch a leak into your own range, so a corrected opponent turns your positive expectation negative
l4hu-counter-strategies-q10.explanation: The larger the deviation, the wider your own attack surface. If the opponent corrects a 60% fold rate back to 50%, your high-frequency bluffing turns from profit into donation — so the size is capped by "you still do not lose after the correction".

l4hu-bn-opening-ex1.title: Standard HU Button Min-Raise
reasoning: 98s is a standard open in HU (on the button), about 48% equity vs the BB's wide defense range
Min-raise steals plus postflop flush/straight potential
The SB acts last postflop with position, and the small size makes postflop pot control easy
l4hu-bn-opening-ex1.mistakeReasoning: Playing HU with full-ring standards wastes the button's opening advantage. 98s has enough value in HU — min-raise actively.

l4hu-bn-opening-ex2.title: Opponent Folds 55%: Still min-raise, Do Not Size Up
reasoning: The BB folds 55%, so the pure steal EV = 0.55 x 1.5 - 0.45 x 1.5 = +0.15BB, just past the 50% break-even line
The same fold rate against a 2.5BB size needs 57.1% to break even (2 / 3.5), so 55% is no longer enough
Q7s keeps position postflop with flush and straight potential, so the opening value does not depend on the steal itself
l4hu-bn-opening-ex2.mistakeAction: Raise to 2.5BB ("more folds means steal harder")
l4hu-bn-opening-ex2.mistakeReasoning: A 55% fold rate only supports the 50% min-raise threshold; at 2.5BB the break-even line rises to 57.1%, this steal segment turns negative, and the extra 0.5BB also makes postflop pot control harder.

l4hu-bn-opening-ex3.title: Only 35% Folds: Open Anyway With a Negative Pure Steal
reasoning: The BB folds 35%, so the pure steal EV = 0.35 x 1.5 - 0.65 x 1.5 = -0.45BB
That -0.45BB is the ceiling cost of opening, not the final result: postflop position plus ace-high with flush potential recover 0.45BB and turn it positive

l4hu-bn-opening-ex3.mistakeAction: Open-shove ("if the steal loses, just shove")
l4hu-bn-opening-ex3.mistakeReasoning: At a 35% fold rate a shove locks the calling range onto strong hands; risking 100BB to plug a 0.45BB theoretical gap is wildly out of proportion.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-ex1.title: BB Marginal EV Call vs the SB's Wide Open
reasoning: Q6s has about 45% equity vs the SB's ~80% opening range
Calling 1BB into a 4BB total pot (SB 2 + BB 1 + the call 1) needs 1÷4 = 25% — a surplus of about 20 points
The BB has the final say preflop and the dead money brings odds, so even marginal hands defend profitably
l4hu-ev-adjustments-ex1.mistakeReasoning: In HU versus the SB's wide range, Q6s's +EV call is hidden by full-ring memory. The BB's preflop final say and pot odds make marginal hands defensible.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-ex2.title: Flop Flush Draw: Two-Street Equity Beats the Half-Pot Price
reasoning: Required equity = 2 / (4 + 2 + 2) = 25%, with 8BB in the pot after the call
KsQs on Js7s2h has a flush draw with 9 outs: the two-street chance is 1 - (38/47) x (37/46) = about 35%, above 25%
Add two overcards and a backdoor straight, and implied odds make the long-run expectation of calling clearly positive
l4hu-ev-adjustments-ex2.mistakeAction: Fold ("one street is only 19%, short of 25%")
l4hu-ev-adjustments-ex2.mistakeReasoning: The single-street 9/47 = about 19% simply halves the two-street equity; a flop call buys both the turn and the river card, so rejecting it on one-street numbers systematically throws away +EV draws.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-ex3.title: Facing a 2.5BB Open: the Calling Line Rises From 25% to 30%
reasoning: Required equity = 1.5 / (1.5 + 2 + 1.5) = 1.5 / 5 = 30% (5BB in the pot after the call)
T8s has about 42% against a SB opening range of roughly 80%, still a surplus of about 12 points
Moving the open from 2BB to 2.5BB only lifts the calling line from 25% to 30%, far below the real equity of a suited connector
l4hu-ev-adjustments-ex3.mistakeReasoning: Treating a bigger open as a doubled price: the real price is only 1.5 / 5 = 30% while the suited connector has 42%, so folding hands the positive expectation to the opponent.

l4hu-gto-basics-ex1.title: HU BB Equilibrium Defense vs an SB Open
reasoning: 65s has about 42% equity vs the SB's ~80% opening range
Calling 1BB into a 4BB total pot (SB 2 + BB 1 + the call 1) needs 1÷4 = 25% — a surplus of about 17 points

l4hu-gto-basics-ex1.mistakeReasoning: The HU BB should defend wide against the SB's wide range; 65s is a standard call. Full-ring standards throw away the preflop information and pot-odds edge.

l4hu-gto-basics-ex2.title: High-Frequency Checking Out of Position on the Flop
reasoning: The BB acts first postflop; Q9 on K-8-3 is only second pair plus a backdoor flush, a medium-strength hand that checks most of the time in equilibrium
Preflop the SB is the aggressor and holds position, so the K-high board range advantage belongs to it; forcing the issue only turns a medium hand into a semi-bluff
Checking keeps the option to call one continuation bet, which fits equilibrium better than building a pot yourself: this line neither surrenders equity nor exposes your range
l4hu-gto-basics-ex2.mistakeReasoning: Leading out with second pair on a K-high board turns a medium hand into a semi-bluff: running into the Kx and stronger hands in the opponent range leaves only the loss of being raised.

l4hu-gto-basics-ex3.title: Half-Pot River: the 3:1 Value-to-Bluff Ratio
reasoning: AK on K-9-4-2-7 is top pair top kicker, and a half-pot river bet is the standard value line
The half-pot value-to-bluff ratio is 3:1: three value hands per bluff, which leaves the opponent exactly indifferent on a 25% calling line
Size and range fit together: half pot pushes the opponent calling line to 5.5 / (11 + 5.5 + 5.5) = 25%, and every medium pair in its range sits on that line
l4hu-gto-basics-ex3.mistakeReasoning: A pot-sized bet demands a 50% defence and lifts the calling line to 33.3%, so value:bluff becomes 2:1; fewer hands in the range can pay you, which reduces a value hand to one that only gets called by better.

l4hu-counter-strategies-ex1.title: Countering an Over-Folding Opponent

Countering over-folding: raise opening frequency
l4hu-counter-strategies-ex1.mistakeReasoning: Against an over-folding opponent, marginal hands profit through stealing; folding wastes the countering opportunity.

l4hu-counter-strategies-ex2.title: Countering a Calling Station: Thin Value, Not Bluffs
reasoning: The BB does not fold postflop (fold rate below 25%): a pure bluff has no fold equity to earn, so value betting is the only direction with profit
KQ is top pair with a good kicker on K-9-4, i.e. a thin value hand; 1/3 pot lets weaker pairs, 9x and draws call cheaply
When the opponent is willing to pay, a small size raises the number of calls and beats one big bet in long-run expectation
l4hu-counter-strategies-ex2.mistakeReasoning: Bluffing pot-sized into a calling station hands chips to someone who never folds; when he does not fold, your bluff density is pure loss.

l4hu-counter-strategies-ex3.title: Countering Over-CBetting: Check-Raise the Overpair
reasoning: The SB continuation-bet frequency is 80% (equilibrium is about 45%-55%): its betting range carries plenty of air, so the overpair is a value raise here
With 5.3BB in the pot, raising to 4BB only needs a fold 4 / (5.3 + 4) = about 43% of the time to break even, and its fold rate against a raise is above 50%
99 is far ahead of the middle of the betting range on 8-5-2, so a value raise both collects the pot and keeps pressure on the turn
l4hu-counter-strategies-ex3.mistakeReasoning: Against a high-frequency continuation bettor, calling hands the initiative back: after calling the flop you face a second barrel on the turn and get pushed off more easily.
